<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">Cross-Embodiment Offline Reinforcement Learning for Heterogeneous Robot Datasets</h1>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Scalable robot policy pre-training has been hindered by the high cost of collecting high-quality demonstrations for each platform. In this study, we address this issue by uniting offline reinforcement learning (offline RL) with cross-embodiment learning. Offline RL leverages both expert and abundant suboptimal data, and cross-embodiment learning aggregates heterogeneous robot trajectories across diverse morphologies to acquire universal control priors. We perform a systematic analysis of this offline RL and cross-embodiment paradigm, providing a principled understanding of its strengths and limitations. To evaluate this offline RL and cross-embodiment paradigm, we construct a suite of locomotion datasets spanning 16 distinct robot platforms. Our experiments confirm that this combined approach excels at pre-training with datasets rich in suboptimal trajectories, outperforming pure behavior cloning. However, as the proportion of suboptimal data and the number of robot types increase, we observe that conflicting gradients across morphologies begin to impede learning. To mitigate this, we introduce an embodiment-based grouping strategy in which robots are clustered by morphological similarity and the model is updated with a group gradient. This simple, static grouping substantially reduces inter-robot conflicts and outperforms existing conflict-resolution methods.</p>
  
</div>
<div id="p1" class="ltx_para">

</table>
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In recent years, breakthroughs across many areas of machine learning have been driven by scaling up both the size of the model and the dataset. In particular, large language models (LLM) and vision-language models (VLM) pre-trained on the web-scale, diverse and massive data have become capable of solving a wide variety of linguistic and visual tasks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">OpenAI, 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gemini Team, 2023</a>)</cite>. Likewise, generative models for image and video generation, as well as music generation, can now produce outputs of unprecedented quality <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rombach et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Singer et al., 2022</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">This trend has also begun to influence robotics, where scaling transformer-based architectures and training them on large, heterogeneous robot datasets have produced ”robot foundation models” capable of multiple tasks within a single model <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Black et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Open X-Embodiment Collaboration, 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Octo Model Team et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kim et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. However, despite the promise of foundation models for robotics, they face a critical limitation. Available demonstration data remain extremely limited compared with the vast text and image corpora that fuel today’s foundation models. Collecting manipulation data is time-consuming and expensive, and each new task requires careful teleoperation, specialized hardware, and often manual labeling, making data scaling difficult.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">To overcome this data bottleneck, researchers have turned to cross-embodiment learning, where a single model is pre-trained on demonstrations from many different robot platforms rather than just one. By pooling heterogeneous data, the model can learn more generalizable control primitives. Building on this, the key practical benefit is adaptability, because a cross-embodiment pre-trained policy can be adapted to new robots with only modest additional data, avoiding per-robot data collection and from-scratch training and thereby lowering costs and speeding deployment. Recent VLA work supports this direction, showing that parameter-efficient and optimized fine-tuning can achieve strong performance and substantial speedups with limited data <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kim et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kim et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">However, these foundation models for robotics have so far been confined to imitation learning, which requires high-quality demonstration data, typically gathered via expert teleoperation, and therefore remains costly for each individual robot. To overcome this limitation, there is growing attention on offline reinforcement learning (offline RL) as a pre-training method. Offline RL can leverage not only expert demonstrations but also suboptimal data, enabling policy learning that can surpass pure imitation learning in settings where high-quality data are difficult to acquire, such as robotics <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Levine et al., 2020</a>)</cite>. For example, Q-Transformer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chebotar et al., 2023</a>)</cite> demonstrates that, when offline RL is applied to large-scale robotic datasets containing suboptimal trajectories, the model can outperform behavior cloning (BC), one of the most widely used approaches to imitation learning. This suggests a natural complementarity. By combining cross-embodiment learning with offline RL, one could exploit heterogeneous robot data and both expert and suboptimal data to dramatically expand the pool of data usable for pre-training. However, this promising combination remains largely unexplored, and there is no established methodology or systematic analysis.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">The contribution of this paper is an empirical study that systematically investigates the challenges and potential of cross-embodiment offline RL. We present a new benchmark and analysis of pre-training combining offline RL with cross-embodiment learning on data collected from up to 16 different robot platforms. Our experiments reveal two key findings: (i) under conditions with substantial suboptimal data, the combined cross-embodiment and offline RL approach outperforms imitation learning, and (ii) as the proportion of suboptimal data and the number of robot types increase, improving performance becomes difficult for particular embodiments under naive offline RL. We analyze this phenomenon and find that, in cross-embodiment learning, each robot’s gradients conflict and cause some robots’ gradients to vanish. This phenomenon leads to a degraded performance. To address this, we propose a novel group-task update strategy based on robot embodiment information. We encode each robot as a morphology graph, compute pairwise distances, and cluster robots accordingly. We then update the policy group by group, sequentially applying an actor update using only the samples of the group. This grouping mitigates gradient conflicts and yields substantial performance gains in settings with high suboptimal data ratios where standard offline RL stalls.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent"><span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="S1.p6.pic1" class="ltx_picture" height="299.6" overflow="visible" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 550 299.6" width="550"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="0.4pt" transform="translate(0,299.6) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0)"><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#4594C1;" fill="#4594C1" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 0 0 L 0 299.6 L 550 299.6 L 550 0 Z"></path></g><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#F0F6FA;" fill="#F0F6FA" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 7.87 0 L 7.87 299.6 L 550 299.6 L 550 0 Z"></path></g><g fill-opacity="1.0" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 19.68 250.24)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:37.54em;--ltx-fo-height:2.78em;--ltx-fo-depth:17.3em;font-size:10pt;" height="277.9" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 38.51)" width="519.45"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content">
<span id="S1.p6.pic1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_minipage ltx_align_bottom" style="width:37.54em;">
<span id="S1.p6.pic1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.p6.pic1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">This paper makes the following contributions:</span></span>
<span id="S1.I1" class="ltx_enumerate">
<span id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<span id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<span id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">We introduce and analyze the new benchmark that combines offline RL with cross-embodiment learning across up to 16 distinct robot platforms.</span></span>
</span></span>
<span id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<span id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">We show that offline RL with cross-embodiment outperforms BC when suboptimal trajectories dominate, and that the pre-trained model can learn representations that markedly accelerate fine-tuning on previously unseen robots.</span></span>
</span></span>
<span id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">3.</span> 
<span id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<span id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">We find positive transfer among morphologically similar robots, while demonstrating that increasing the suboptimal-data ratio and the number/diversity of robots amplifies inter-robot gradient conflicts, which in turn induces negative transfer.</span></span>
</span></span>
<span id="S1.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">4.</span> 
<span id="S1.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<span id="S1.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">To mitigate these conflicts, we propose a simple, static grouping strategy that represents each robot as a morphology graph and clusters robots by graph-based distances; performing group-wise policy updates reduces gradient interference and yields large gains, up to 39.8% improvement, especially under high suboptimal-data conditions.</span></span>
</span></span>
</span>
</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Related Works</h2>

<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1 </span>Offline RL</h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Offline RL aims to learn a policy that maximizes cumulative reward using only a static dataset of environment interactions without further online interaction <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Levine et al., 2020</a>)</cite>. Compared to BC, which simply mimics the trajectories of the dataset, offline RL can stitch together suboptimal segments to produce better performance when the dataset contains a mix of expert and suboptimal data <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kostrikov et al., 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kumar et al., 2020</a>)</cite>. For example, implicit Q-learning (IQL) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kostrikov et al., 2021</a>)</cite> first fits a state value function <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V_{\psi}(s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>ψ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V_{\psi}(s)</annotation></semantics></math> via expectile regression to capture an upper expectile of the return distribution; it then uses the learned <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V_{\psi}(s^{\prime})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>ψ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V_{\psi}(s^{\prime})</annotation></semantics></math> as the TD target for updating a state–action value function <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Q_{\theta}(s,a)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>Q</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q_{\theta}(s,a)</annotation></semantics></math>. Finally, the policy <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{\phi}(a\mid s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{\phi}(a\mid s)</annotation></semantics></math> is extracted via advantage-weighted BC, avoiding any need to evaluate out-of-distribution actions. This pipeline enables IQL to leverage suboptimal trajectories effectively and achieve strong performance without explicit policy constraints. In this work, we adopt offline RL as our pre-training paradigm to broaden robotic data, especially suboptimal data that can be exploited for foundation model learning in robotics.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2 </span>Cross-Embodiment Learning</h3>

<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Cross-embodiment learning trains a single network on data collected from multiple robot morphologies, enabling transfer of control priors across platforms. Since collecting large datasets for any single robot is costly, pre-training on heterogeneous robot data has become a popular strategy to improve generalization capability <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Open X-Embodiment Collaboration, 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Octo Model Team et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Black et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kim et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. However, existing cross-embodiment foundation models rely almost exclusively on imitation learning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Open X-Embodiment Collaboration, 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Octo Model Team et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, and there has been little work combining cross-embodiment pre-training with offline RL. While <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Nakamoto et al. (2024)</a></cite> applied offline RL to data from two robot platforms, they did not analyze any cross-embodiment effects. Similarly, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Springenberg et al. (2024)</a></cite> conducted offline RL on a dataset comprising two manipulators and several toy tasks but did not investigate the benefits or challenges of learning from many distinct embodiments simultaneously. To fill this gap, we introduce the new benchmark that systematically combines offline RL with cross-embodiment learning, analyze the interactions between these paradigms, and propose methods to mitigate the challenges that arise when pooling heterogeneous and often suboptimal robot data.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Experimental Setup</h2>

<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Problem Setting</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We study multi-embodiment offline RL, where a single policy must control multiple robot morphologies under a common state–action interface. Unlike the standard multi-task RL setting, where a single robot embodiment solves multiple tasks with different rewards or goals, here multiple robot embodiments solve a common locomotion objective and reward functions that share the same components but may use embodiment-specific weights. Such settings have been referred to as cross-embodiment or multi-embodiment learning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Open X-Embodiment Collaboration, 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bohlinger et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. In this work, we follow this terminology and refer to our setting as cross-embodiment offline RL. Concretely, let <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒯</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{T}</annotation></semantics></math> denote a finite set of robot embodiments (e.g., different quadrupeds, bipeds, hexapods) and let <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f^{\mathrm{morph}}:\mathcal{T}\to\mathbb{R}^{d_{m}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>f</mi><mi>morph</mi></msup><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒯</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>m</mi></msub></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f^{\mathrm{morph}}:\mathcal{T}\to\mathbb{R}^{d_{m}}</annotation></semantics></math> map each embodiment index <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math> to a morphology descriptor <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f^{\mathrm{morph}}(\tau)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>f</mi><mi>morph</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f^{\mathrm{morph}}(\tau)</annotation></semantics></math>. Each embodiment <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau\in\mathcal{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒯</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau\in\mathcal{T}</annotation></semantics></math> induces an MDP <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\mathcal{M}_{\tau}=\bigl(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},p_{0,\tau}(s),P_{\tau}(\cdot\!\mid\!s,a),r_{\tau}(s,a),\gamma\bigr)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mi>τ</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><mo>,</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>τ</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mpadded style="width:0.108em;" width="0.108em"><mo lspace="0em">⋅</mo></mpadded><mpadded style="width:0.219em;" width="0.219em"><mo>∣</mo></mpadded><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>τ</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>γ</mi><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{M}_{\tau}=\bigl(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},p_{0,\tau}(s),P_{\tau}(\cdot\!\mid\!s,a),r_{\tau}(s,a),\gamma\bigr)</annotation></semantics></math>
where <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{S}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d_{s}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><mo>⊂</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>s</mi></msub></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{S}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d_{s}}</annotation></semantics></math> is the shared observation space (joint angles, velocities, etc.), <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{A}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d_{a}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi><mo>⊂</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>a</mi></msub></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{A}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d_{a}}</annotation></semantics></math> is the continuous control space, <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{0,\tau}(s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{0,\tau}(s)</annotation></semantics></math> is the embodiment-specific distribution over initial states, <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P_{\tau}(s^{\prime}\!\mid\!s,a)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>τ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mpadded style="width:0.052em;" width="0.052em"><mo fence="true" lspace="0em">∣</mo></mpadded><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P_{\tau}(s^{\prime}\!\mid\!s,a)</annotation></semantics></math> is the embodiment-specific environment dynamics, <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r_{\tau}(s,a)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>τ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r_{\tau}(s,a)</annotation></semantics></math> is a dense embodiment-specific reward and <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma\in(0,1)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>γ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma\in(0,1)</annotation></semantics></math> is the discount factor. Episodes may end according to a terminal condition encoded in the transition tuples through a termination indicator <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{t}\in\{0,1\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{t}\in\{0,1\}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We assume access to a pooled offline dataset <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}\;=\;\bigcup_{\tau\in\mathcal{T}}\{(s_{t},a_{t},s_{t+1},r_{t},d_{t})\}_{t=1}^{N_{\tau}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mo lspace="0.558em" rspace="0.391em">=</mo><mrow><msub><mo rspace="0em">⋃</mo><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒯</mi></mrow></msub><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>τ</mi></msub></msubsup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}\;=\;\bigcup_{\tau\in\mathcal{T}}\{(s_{t},a_{t},s_{t+1},r_{t},d_{t})\}_{t=1}^{N_{\tau}}</annotation></semantics></math> generated by an unknown behavior policy <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{\beta}(a\mid s,f^{\mathrm{morph}}(\tau))" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>β</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><msup><mi>f</mi><mi>morph</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{\beta}(a\mid s,f^{\mathrm{morph}}(\tau))</annotation></semantics></math>. Our goal is to learn a single parameterized policy <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s,f^{\mathrm{morph}}(\tau))" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><msup><mi>f</mi><mi>morph</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s,f^{\mathrm{morph}}(\tau))</annotation></semantics></math> that maximizes the expected cumulative discounted return over all embodiments <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{R}=\sum_{\tau}\sum{{}_{t=0}^{T}\gamma^{t}r_{\tau}(s_{t},a_{t})}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℛ</mi><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><msub><mo rspace="0em">∑</mo><mi>τ</mi></msub><mrow><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mmultiscripts><mi>γ</mi><mrow></mrow><mi>t</mi><mprescripts></mprescripts><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mi>T</mi></mmultiscripts><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>τ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{R}=\sum_{\tau}\sum{{}_{t=0}^{T}\gamma^{t}r_{\tau}(s_{t},a_{t})}</annotation></semantics></math>, using only <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}</annotation></semantics></math>. Rather than providing the policy with a one-hot embodiment index, we rely on morphology features (size, mass, link lengths, etc.), which we formalize as the descriptor <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f^{\mathrm{morph}}(\tau)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>f</mi><mi>morph</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f^{\mathrm{morph}}(\tau)</annotation></semantics></math>. In this way, the same policy <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s,f^{\mathrm{morph}}(\tau))" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><msup><mi>f</mi><mi>morph</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s,f^{\mathrm{morph}}(\tau))</annotation></semantics></math> can generalize across embodiments by conditioning on these universal state features.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Environments and Dataset</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To facilitate cross-embodiment pre-training under an offline RL paradigm, we constructed a new locomotion dataset within the MuJoCo <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Todorov et al., 2012</a>)</cite> simulation environment, following the walking tasks of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bohlinger et al. (2024)</a></cite>. Our dataset includes 16 distinct robot platforms, including nine quadrupeds, six bipeds, and one hexapod, each trained by Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schulman et al., 2017</a>)</cite>. During training, we record the tuple <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(s_{t},\,a_{t},\,s_{t+1},\,r_{t},\,d_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(s_{t},\,a_{t},\,s_{t+1},\,r_{t},\,d_{t})</annotation></semantics></math> at each time step to capture the state, action, next state, reward, and termination signals.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For each robot, we curate six variants of 1 M–step datasets, divided by data quality:</p>
<ul id="S3.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S3.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Expert data</span>: 1 M steps collected by rolling out the fully converged PPO policy.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Expert Replay data</span>: all interaction steps from training start until expert-level performance (<math id="S3.I1.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim 500\,\mathrm{M}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mn>500</mn><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim 500\,\mathrm{M}</annotation></semantics></math> steps in total), uniformly subsampled to <math id="S3.I1.i2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1\,\mathrm{M}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1\,\mathrm{M}</annotation></semantics></math> steps to bound dataset size.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">70% Suboptimal Replay data</span>: 700 k steps drawn from the early (suboptimal) phase of PPO training, mixed with 300 k steps from the late (expert-like) phase, totaling 1 M steps.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.2" class="ltx_p">Each of these Expert, Expert Replay, and 70% Suboptimal Replay datasets is provided in two walking-direction variants, Forward and Backward.
In the Forward variant, the robot is commanded to walk forward at <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1\,\mathrm{m/s}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow><mo>/</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1\,\mathrm{m/s}</annotation></semantics></math>, whereas in the Backward variant the commanded base velocity is <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="-1\,\mathrm{m/s}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mi>m</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-1\,\mathrm{m/s}</annotation></semantics></math>.
The reward in both cases is the same dense locomotion reward, and the tasks differ only in the commanded walking direction. See Appendix <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B Dataset Construction Details ‣ Cross-Embodiment Offline Reinforcement Learning for Heterogeneous Robot Datasets" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a> for dataset construction details and Appendix <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C Dataset Detail ‣ Cross-Embodiment Offline Reinforcement Learning for Heterogeneous Robot Datasets" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a> for reward distributions.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3 </span>Network Architecture</h3>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we present our approach to cross-embodiment learning in an offline RL setting. The central challenge is to train a single network across robots whose state and action dimensions differ. To address this, we adopt the URMA architecture <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bohlinger et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, which enables multiple robots to share a single policy and state value function. URMA factorizes each observation into an embodiment-agnostic general part <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="o_{g}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>g</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">o_{g}</annotation></semantics></math> and a robot-specific part. For locomotion, the robot-specific stream is further split into variable-length sets of joint and foot observations, <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{o_{j}\}_{j\in J(\tau)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mi>J</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{o_{j}\}_{j\in J(\tau)}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{o_{f}\}_{f\in F(\tau)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>f</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{o_{f}\}_{f\in F(\tau)}</annotation></semantics></math>. Descriptor-conditioned attention aggregates each set into fixed-size latents, which are concatenated with <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="o_{g}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>g</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">o_{g}</annotation></semantics></math> to form a morphology-agnostic core representation. To facilitate offline RL, we further extend URMA by introducing a state–action value function (<math id="S3.SS3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Q" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>Q</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q</annotation></semantics></math>-function). Specifically, we encode each action with an action encoder to obtain a latent action vector, which we then concatenate with the latent representation of the URMA encoder. See Appendix <a href="#A4" title="Appendix D Architecture Details ‣ Cross-Embodiment Offline Reinforcement Learning for Heterogeneous Robot Datasets" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D</span></a> for architectural details.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Analysis of Standard Offline RL Algorithm in Cross-Embodiment Offline RL</h2>

<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Comparison of Behavior Cloning and Offline RL</h3>

<td id="S4.T1.2.8.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;">52.05</td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Here, we compare BC, widely used in cross-embodiment training of foundational robot models, with offline RL. To date, applications of offline RL to robot foundation models have been rare, owing to the difficulty of learning from unlabeled interaction data; thus, a rigorous evaluation is necessary. Table <a href="#S4.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 4.1 Comparison of Behavior Cloning and Offline RL ‣ 4 Analysis of Standard Offline RL Algorithm in Cross-Embodiment Offline RL ‣ Cross-Embodiment Offline Reinforcement Learning for Heterogeneous Robot Datasets" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> reports the performance of BC and implicit Q-learning (IQL) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kostrikov et al., 2021</a>)</cite>, the commonly used offline RL method. On datasets with relatively uniform behavioral quality (for example, Forward Expert and Backward Expert), BC and offline RL achieve comparable results. In contrast, on datasets containing predominantly suboptimal trajectories, specifically 70% Suboptimal Replay Forward and Expert Replay data, offline RL methods surpass BC. This finding mirrors the results reported on benchmarks like D4RL <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fu et al., 2020</a>)</cite> and confirms that offline RL remains robust even when datasets include significant suboptimal data in a cross-embodiment context.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Effects of Cross-Embodiment Pre-training</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In the next experiment, we now evaluate how cross-embodiment pre-training impacts the performance of single-embodiment fine-tuning with offline RL. Figure <a href="#S4.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 4.2 Effects of Cross-Embodiment Pre-training ‣ 4 Analysis of Standard Offline RL Algorithm in Cross-Embodiment Offline RL ‣ Cross-Embodiment Offline Reinforcement Learning for Heterogeneous Robot Datasets" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> shows the learning curves for a “leave-one-out” experiment. We pre-train via offline RL on a dataset excluding one robot, then fine-tune that robot with pre-trained networks, comparing it to a model trained without cross-embodiment pre-training. The model pre-trained with cross-embodiment data converges markedly faster. The results show that, for the quadrupedal robot Badger as well as for the bipedal robots Unitree G1 and Cassie, the network pre-trained via a cross-embodiment dataset is able to learn an effective policy more rapidly. These results demonstrate that cross-embodiment learning serves as a highly effective pre-training strategy in offline RL.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F1" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18025v1/learning_curves_all_red_green.svg" id="S4.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:548/153;" width="548" height="153"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 1: </span>Comparison of learning curves between cross-embodiment pre-trained networks and networks trained without cross-embodiment pre-training for Badger, Unitree G1, and Cassie.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>Positive and Negative Transfer in Cross-Embodiment Learning with Suboptimal Data</h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we first compare the final performance of models trained on each robot in isolation with a model trained via cross-embodiment learning. Table <a href="#S4.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 4.3 Positive and Negative Transfer in Cross-Embodiment Learning with Suboptimal Data ‣ 4 Analysis of Standard Offline RL Algorithm in Cross-Embodiment Offline RL ‣ Cross-Embodiment Offline Reinforcement Learning for Heterogeneous Robot Datasets" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> shows the final rewards achieved by IQL when trained via cross-embodiment on the Expert Forward and 70% Suboptimal Replay Forward datasets, along with the rewards obtained by models trained separately on each robot.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In the Expert Forward dataset, the cross-embodiment models learn just as effectively as the single-robot models. However, an examination of the 70% Suboptimal Replay Forward dataset, which contains a large proportion of suboptimal data, reveals a different result. Although the average performance of cross-embodiment models falls below that of isolated models, certain quadrupedal robots, Unitree A1, Unitree Go1, Unitree Go2, and Badger, show substantial performance gains. This suggests that positive transfer occurs among the quadrupeds, likely because they contribute the largest share of data to the dataset.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">By contrast, bipedal robots such as Unitree H1 and Unitree G1, which have relatively little similar-embodiment data in the dataset, suffer pronounced performance degradation under cross-embodiment learning compared to their isolated training. Because this negative transfer does not appear when using suboptimal data without cross-embodiment or when training on the Expert dataset which contains fewer suboptimal trajectories, we conclude that negative transfer emerges only when a dataset combines large amounts of suboptimal data with the cross-embodiment training regime.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Together these results show that the combination of cross-embodiment learning and offline RL can yield both positive and negative transfer. Negative transfer is most likely when suboptimal trajectories dominate and embodiment diversity is high. These findings indicate that effective cross-embodiment learning requires methods that minimize negative transfer while maximizing positive transfer.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.SS3.fig3" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">

<tbody class="ltx_tbody">
<tr id="S4.T2.1.2" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="S4.T2.1.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row ltx_border_t" style="padding:-0.25pt 4.0pt;">unitree_a1</th>

<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Gradient Conflicts and Resolution via Embodiment-Based Grouping</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we analyze why combining large amounts of suboptimal data with cross-embodiment learning fails to yield performance improvements. Our empirical results indicate that gradient conflict is a primary cause of negative transfer. To address this issue, we propose a novel mitigation strategy that groups robots according to their embodiment, thus reducing gradient conflicts.</p>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.1 </span>Gradient Conflicts among Robots</h3>

<div id="S5.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We hypothesize that when suboptimal data dominate the training set, simultaneous cross-embodiment learning induces negative transfer through conflicting policy gradients across robots. In particular, bipedal robots (e.g., Unitree H1 and Unitree G1) are most affected, since the dataset contains relatively little data from similarly embodied robots; these gradient conflicts can effectively cancel useful updates and stall learning.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To quantify this effect, we analyze the actor gradients arising from advantage-weighted regression <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kostrikov et al., 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Nair et al., 2020</a>)</cite>. For each embodiment <math id="S5.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math>, we define the actor objective</p>
<table id="S5.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S5.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}^{\pi}_{\tau}(\theta)=-\mathbb{E}_{(s,a)\sim\mathcal{D}_{\tau}}\!\left[w(s,a)\,\log\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s)\right],\qquad w(s,a)\;=\;\exp\!\big(\beta(Q(s,a)-V(s))\big)." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>∼</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mi>τ</mi></msub></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo rspace="0.280em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.558em">=</mo><mrow><mpadded style="width:1.370em;" stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>V</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}^{\pi}_{\tau}(\theta)=-\mathbb{E}_{(s,a)\sim\mathcal{D}_{\tau}}\!\left[w(s,a)\,\log\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s)\right],\qquad w(s,a)\;=\;\exp\!\big(\beta(Q(s,a)-V(s))\big).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S5.SS1.p2.2" class="ltx_p">in which <math id="S5.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Q(s,a)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>Q</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q(s,a)</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the learned state-action value function and <math id="S5.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V(s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>V</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V(s)</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the learned state value function. We denote the per-embodiment actor gradient by <math id="S5.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g_{\tau}\;=\;\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}^{\pi}_{\tau}(\theta)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>g</mi><mi>τ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.558em" rspace="0.558em">=</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mo rspace="0.167em">∇</mo><mi>θ</mi></msub><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mi>τ</mi><mi>π</mi></msubsup></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g_{\tau}\;=\;\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}^{\pi}_{\tau}(\theta)</annotation></semantics></math> and measure inter-embodiment alignment via the pairwise cosine similarity</p>
<table id="S5.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S5.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C[\tau_{i},\tau_{j}]\;=\;\frac{\langle g_{\tau_{i}},\,g_{\tau_{j}}\rangle}{\|g_{\tau_{i}}\|\,\|g_{\tau_{j}}\|}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msub><mi>τ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>τ</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow><mo rspace="0.280em" stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.558em">=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy="false">⟨</mo><mrow><msub><mi>g</mi><msub><mi>τ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></msub><mo rspace="0.337em">,</mo><msub><mi>g</mi><msub><mi>τ</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">⟩</mo></mrow><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msub><mi>g</mi><msub><mi>τ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></msub><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msub><mi>g</mi><msub><mi>τ</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></msub><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C[\tau_{i},\tau_{j}]\;=\;\frac{\langle g_{\tau_{i}},\,g_{\tau_{j}}\rangle}{\|g_{\tau_{i}}\|\,\|g_{\tau_{j}}\|}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S4.F3.sf1" title="In 4.3 Positive and Negative Transfer in Cross-Embodiment Learning with Suboptimal Data ‣ 4 Analysis of Standard Offline RL Algorithm in Cross-Embodiment Offline RL ‣ Cross-Embodiment Offline Reinforcement Learning for Heterogeneous Robot Datasets" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3(a)</span></a> reports, during training, the proportion of pairwise cosine similarities that are negative (<math id="S5.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C[\tau_{i},\tau_{j}]&lt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msub><mi>τ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>τ</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C[\tau_{i},\tau_{j}]&lt;0</annotation></semantics></math>) for three datasets: Expert Forward and 30% and 70% Suboptimal Replay Forward. As the proportion of suboptimal data increases, the share of negative cosines increases, indicating more frequent gradient conflicts between robots.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">To further investigate the relationship between transfer and gradient conflicts, we compute the correlation between each robot’s transfer gain and its average gradient cosine similarity with all other robots in the 70% Suboptimal Replay dataset. We define the transfer gain as the change in average return induced by cross-embodiment training compared to single-embodiment training. We use robots with substantial transfer gain (absolute change in return greater than <math id="S5.SS1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>10</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10</annotation></semantics></math>), as highlighted in Table <a href="#S4.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 4.3 Positive and Negative Transfer in Cross-Embodiment Learning with Suboptimal Data ‣ 4 Analysis of Standard Offline RL Algorithm in Cross-Embodiment Offline RL ‣ Cross-Embodiment Offline Reinforcement Learning for Heterogeneous Robot Datasets" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>. The resulting correlation, <math id="S5.SS1.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r=0.815" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.815</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r=0.815</annotation></semantics></math>, indicates a strong positive relationship: robots that exhibit positive transfer have more aligned gradients, whereas those with large negative transfer exhibit greater gradient conflict. These findings confirm that gradient conflicts underlie the negative transfer observed when applying cross-embodiment learning to datasets rich in suboptimal data.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Next, we examine how gradient conflicts change as the number and diversity of robots increase (Figure <a href="#S4.F3.sf2" title="In 4.3 Positive and Negative Transfer in Cross-Embodiment Learning with Suboptimal Data ‣ 4 Analysis of Standard Offline RL Algorithm in Cross-Embodiment Offline RL ‣ Cross-Embodiment Offline Reinforcement Learning for Heterogeneous Robot Datasets" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3(b)</span></a>). Using the 70% Suboptimal Forward dataset, we progressively expanded the set of included robots: a relatively similar group (Unitree A1, Go1, Go2), then all nine quadrupeds, and finally all 16 robots. As we include more diverse robots, each robot exhibits a higher fraction of negative pairwise cosine similarities with the others (<math id="S5.SS1.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C&lt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C&lt;0</annotation></semantics></math>). In other words, greater embodiment diversity leads to more negative cosine similarities and more frequent gradient conflicts, making negative transfer more likely. Additional distributional analysis of these effects is provided in Appendix <a href="#A6" title="Appendix F Detailed analysis of gradient conflicts ‣ Cross-Embodiment Offline Reinforcement Learning for Heterogeneous Robot Datasets" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F</span></a>, and Appendix <a href="#A7.SS1" title="G.1 Gradient conflicts under TD3+BC. ‣ Appendix G Additional correlation analysis for TD3+BC ‣ Cross-Embodiment Offline Reinforcement Learning for Heterogeneous Robot Datasets" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">G.1</span></a> shows that the same qualitative relationships between the amount of suboptimal data, the number and diversity of embodiments, and how often gradient conflicts occur also hold for another offline RL algorithm, TD3+BC <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fujimoto and Gu, 2021</a>)</cite>, suggesting that these phenomena arise more generally in cross-embodiment offline RL.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.F4" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_3">
<figure id="S5.F4.sf1" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><img src="2602.18025v1/images/etas_fixed.png" id="S5.F4.sf1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:548/533;" width="548" height="533" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">(a) </span>Embodiment-based similarity matrix</figcaption>
</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_3">
<figure id="S5.F4.sf2" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><img src="2602.18025v1/images/grad_matrix_expert_symlog.png" id="S5.F4.sf2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:548/526;" width="548" height="526" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">(b) </span>Average gradient cosine similarity matrix</figcaption>
</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_3">
<figure id="S5.F4.sf3" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><img src="2602.18025v1/images/emsim_grad_scatter.png" id="S5.F4.sf3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:548/547;" width="548" height="547" alt="Refer to caption">

</figure></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 4: </span>(a) Embodiment-based similarity matrix (1 - min-max-normalized FGW distance between robot pairs);

(c) Scatter plot of embodiment-based similarity and mean gradient cosine similarity for all robot pairs.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.2 </span>Correlation between Embodiment Distance and the Gradient Conflicts</h3>

<div id="S5.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We now analyze how gradient alignment across robots is captured by morphological similarity. We represent each robot’s embodiment as a graph to quantify inter-robot distances. Nodes correspond to the torso, joints, and feet. Edges connect the torso to adjacent joints, adjacent joints to each other, and each terminal joint to its foot. Node features include relative positions from the torso and control parameters, capturing morphology and actuation. We then compute pairwise distances between these graphs using the Fused Gromov–Wasserstein (FGW) distance <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Vayer et al., 2020</a>)</cite>. Because FGW jointly accounts for both graph structure and node features when computing distances, it is well suited for measuring dissimilarities between these robot embodiment graphs. For visualization and subsequent correlation analysis, we linearly normalize the FGW distance matrix so that all entries lie in the range <math id="S5.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[0,1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[0,1]</annotation></semantics></math>, then convert distances into similarities by plotting <math id="S5.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1-d_{\mathrm{FGW}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>FGW</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1-d_{\mathrm{FGW}}</annotation></semantics></math>, so that larger values correspond to more similar robot pairs. The resulting similarity matrix is shown in Figure <a href="#S5.F4.sf1" title="In Figure 4 ‣ 5.1 Gradient Conflicts among Robots ‣ 5 Gradient Conflicts and Resolution via Embodiment-Based Grouping ‣ Cross-Embodiment Offline Reinforcement Learning for Heterogeneous Robot Datasets" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4(a)</span></a>. Quadrupedal robots cluster closely, for example Unitree Go1, A1, Go2, and Anymal B/C, matches intuition.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We next analyze how these embodiment based distances relate to the gradient conflicts characterized in Section <a href="#S5.SS1" title="5.1 Gradient Conflicts among Robots ‣ 5 Gradient Conflicts and Resolution via Embodiment-Based Grouping ‣ Cross-Embodiment Offline Reinforcement Learning for Heterogeneous Robot Datasets" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.1</span></a> and find that they are strongly correlated. Figure <a href="#S5.F4.sf2" title="In Figure 4 ‣ 5.1 Gradient Conflicts among Robots ‣ 5 Gradient Conflicts and Resolution via Embodiment-Based Grouping ‣ Cross-Embodiment Offline Reinforcement Learning for Heterogeneous Robot Datasets" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4(b)</span></a> presents the average gradient cosine similarity matrix from Section <a href="#S5.SS1" title="5.1 Gradient Conflicts among Robots ‣ 5 Gradient Conflicts and Resolution via Embodiment-Based Grouping ‣ Cross-Embodiment Offline Reinforcement Learning for Heterogeneous Robot Datasets" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.1</span></a>. Figure <a href="#S5.F4.sf3" title="In Figure 4 ‣ 5.1 Gradient Conflicts among Robots ‣ 5 Gradient Conflicts and Resolution via Embodiment-Based Grouping ‣ Cross-Embodiment Offline Reinforcement Learning for Heterogeneous Robot Datasets" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4(c)</span></a> further visualizes this relationship as a scatter plot between embodiment similarity and mean gradient cosine similarity. The Pearson correlation coefficient between these two quantities is <math id="S5.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r=0.63" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.63</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r=0.63</annotation></semantics></math> (<math id="S5.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p=1.26\times 10^{-14}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>1.26</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>14</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p=1.26\times 10^{-14}</annotation></semantics></math>), indicating a statistically significant positive correlation: morphologically similar robot pairs tend to have more aligned policy gradients, whereas morphologically dissimilar pairs exhibit greater gradient conflicts. Repeating the same embodiment similarity analysis with TD3+BC in Appendix <a href="#A7.SS2" title="G.2 Correlation with embodiment similarity ‣ Appendix G Additional correlation analysis for TD3+BC ‣ Cross-Embodiment Offline Reinforcement Learning for Heterogeneous Robot Datasets" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">G.2</span></a> yields a comparable Pearson correlation between embodiment similarity and mean gradient cosine similarity, further supporting that the morphology dependent structure of gradient conflicts is a general property. Motivated by these observations, the next subsection introduces an embodiment grouped offline RL update that explicitly exploits this structure to mitigate gradient conflicts.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.F5" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18025v1/EG_fig_iclr.png" id="S5.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:548/120;" width="548" height="120" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 5: </span>Overview of Embodiment Grouping (EG) for cross-embodiment offline RL.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.3 </span>Embodiment-Grouped Offline RL Update</h3>

<figure id="S5.SS3.fig1" class="ltx_figure ltx_align_floatright" style="width:50%;"><span class="ltx_rule" style="width:100%;height:0.8pt;--ltx-bg-color:black;display:inline-block;"> </span>
<br class="ltx_break ltx_break">
<p id="S5.SS3.fig1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS3.fig1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Algorithm 1</span> Embodiment-Grouped Offline RL</p>
<br class="ltx_break ltx_break"><span class="ltx_rule" style="width:100%;height:0.6pt;--ltx-bg-color:black;display:inline-block;"> </span>

            Robot groups <math id="algx1.l1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{\mathcal{G}_{1},\dots,\mathcal{G}_{M}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi><mi>M</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{\mathcal{G}_{1},\dots,\mathcal{G}_{M}\}</annotation></semantics></math>, dataset <math id="algx1.l1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}</annotation></semantics></math>

              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline">3:</span>
              
              
            <span id="algx1.l3.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">for</span> each outer iteration <span id="algx1.l3.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">do</span>

</div>
<div id="algx1.l4" class="ltx_listingline">
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline">4:</span>
              
              
              Sample global minibatch <math id="algx1.l4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{B}\sim\mathcal{D}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℬ</mi><mo>∼</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{B}\sim\mathcal{D}</annotation></semantics></math>

</div>
<div id="algx1.l5" class="ltx_listingline">
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline">5:</span>
              
              
              Compute <math id="algx1.l5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L_{\text{critic}}(\mathcal{B})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>L</mi><mtext>critic</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℬ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L_{\text{critic}}(\mathcal{B})</annotation></semantics></math>; update <math id="algx1.l5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta_{c}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>θ</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta_{c}</annotation></semantics></math>

</div>
<div id="algx1.l6" class="ltx_listingline">
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline">6:</span>
              
              
              Update target networks

</div>
<div id="algx1.l7" class="ltx_listingline">
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline">7:</span>
              
              
              <math id="algx1.l7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P\leftarrow\mathrm{shuffle}(\{1,\dots,M\})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">←</mo><mrow><mi>shuffle</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P\leftarrow\mathrm{shuffle}(\{1,\dots,M\})</annotation></semantics></math>

</div>
<div id="algx1.l8" class="ltx_listingline">
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline">8:</span>
              
              
              <span id="algx1.l8.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">for</span> <math id="algx1.l8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m\in P" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m\in P</annotation></semantics></math> <span id="algx1.l8.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">do</span>

</div>
<div id="algx1.l9" class="ltx_listingline">
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline">9:</span>
              
              
               <math id="algx1.l9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{B}_{m}\leftarrow\{x\in\mathcal{B}\mid\mathrm{robot}(x)\in\mathcal{G}_{m}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℬ</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">←</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℬ</mi></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>robot</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi><mi>m</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{B}_{m}\leftarrow\{x\in\mathcal{B}\mid\mathrm{robot}(x)\in\mathcal{G}_{m}\}</annotation></semantics></math>

</div>
<div id="algx1.l10" class="ltx_listingline">
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline">10:</span>
              
              
               Compute <math id="algx1.l10.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L_{\pi}(\mathcal{B}_{m})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>π</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℬ</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L_{\pi}(\mathcal{B}_{m})</annotation></semantics></math>; update <math id="algx1.l10.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta_{\pi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>θ</mi><mi>π</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta_{\pi}</annotation></semantics></math>

</div>
<div id="algx1.l11" class="ltx_listingline">
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline">11:</span>
              
              
              <span id="algx1.l11.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">end</span> <span id="algx1.l11.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">for</span>
</div>
<div id="algx1.l12" class="ltx_listingline">
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline">12:</span>
              
              
            <span id="algx1.l12.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">end</span> <span id="algx1.l12.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">for</span>
</div>
</div>
<br class="ltx_break ltx_break"><span class="ltx_rule" style="width:100%;height:0.8pt;--ltx-bg-color:black;display:inline-block;"> </span>
</figure>
<div id="S5.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Based on the analysis in the previous subsection, we hypothesized that preventing gradient conflict would yield more efficient learning. Inspired by selective group updates <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jeong and Yoon, 2025</a>)</cite>, we partition robots into groups before applying actor updates. Concretely, following Section <a href="#S5.SS2" title="5.2 Correlation between Embodiment Distance and the Gradient Conflicts ‣ 5 Gradient Conflicts and Resolution via Embodiment-Based Grouping ‣ Cross-Embodiment Offline Reinforcement Learning for Heterogeneous Robot Datasets" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.2</span></a>, we represent each robot as a graph, compute pairwise FGW distances between robot graphs, and create an embodiment-distance matrix. We then apply hierarchical clustering to this matrix to obtain <math id="S5.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> robot groups, which remain fixed throughout training. Training then proceeds with one global critic update, followed by sequential group-wise actor updates. Figure <a href="#S5.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ 5.2 Correlation between Embodiment Distance and the Gradient Conflicts ‣ 5 Gradient Conflicts and Resolution via Embodiment-Based Grouping ‣ Cross-Embodiment Offline Reinforcement Learning for Heterogeneous Robot Datasets" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> illustrates this full Embodiment Grouping (EG) workflow. Details on the robot graph construction and FGW distance hyperparameters are given in Appendix <a href="#A5" title="Appendix E Embodiment Grouping Details ‣ Cross-Embodiment Offline Reinforcement Learning for Heterogeneous Robot Datasets" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E</span></a>. In the experiments, we also evaluate alternative groupings such as random partitioning and a heuristic split, and we report the comparisons in Section <a href="#S6.SS2" title="6.2 Ablations &amp; Compute-Normalized Analysis ‣ 6 Experimental Evaluation ‣ Cross-Embodiment Offline Reinforcement Learning for Heterogeneous Robot Datasets" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6.2</span></a>.
This pre-specified embodiment-based grouping is simple to implement yet highly effective.
The algorithm is summarized in Algorithm <a href="#S5.SS3" title="5.3 Embodiment-Grouped Offline RL Update ‣ 5 Gradient Conflicts and Resolution via Embodiment-Based Grouping ‣ Cross-Embodiment Offline Reinforcement Learning for Heterogeneous Robot Datasets" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.3</span></a> and can be easily integrated with standard offline RL methods.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Experimental Evaluation</h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our experiments are designed to validate the effectiveness of Embodiment Grouping in two parts. First, we evaluate performance improvements in cross-embodiment offline RL on six datasets containing varying proportions of suboptimal data. We compare eight methods. As single-method baselines, we include Behavior Cloning (BC) using the same network architecture as our offline RL backbones, TD3+BC <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fujimoto and Gu, 2021</a>)</cite> as a strong and widely used offline continuous-control baseline, and implicit Q-learning (IQL). To evaluate existing approaches for mitigating negative transfer, we also test two gradient-conflict–aware IQL variants: IQL+PCGrad, which resolves gradient conflicts via gradient projection <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yu et al., 2020</a>)</cite>, and IQL+SEL, which selectively groups tasks based on dynamic task affinity <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jeong and Yoon, 2025</a>)</cite>. Finally, to assess the effect of our embodiment-based grouping strategy across different learning backbones, we report Embodiment Grouping (EG) counterparts of BC, TD3+BC, and IQL. We denote these variants as BC+EG, TD3+BC+EG, and IQL+EG (ours), respectively. All methods are trained offline and in aggregate use approximately 100 million transition samples per robot for gradient updates.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Second, we conduct ablation studies to isolate the contributions of (i) grouping strategy, comparing random grouping, an intuitive biped / quadruped split and our embodiment-based grouping; (ii) the number of groups <math id="S6.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math>; and (iii) update-count control, for which we report a compute-normalized comparison that matches both total optimizer steps and processed samples across methods. Detailed hyperparameters and training configurations are provided in Appendix <a href="#A9" title="Appendix I Hyperparameters and Training Details ‣ Cross-Embodiment Offline Reinforcement Learning for Heterogeneous Robot Datasets" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">I</span></a>.</p>
</div>
