</figure>
<section id="S6.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">6.1 </span>Grouping Robots by Embodiment Makes Cross-Embodiment Learning Better</h3>

<div id="S6.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this experiment, we evaluate, on our cross-embodiment offline RL benchmark, how much the proposed Embodiment Grouping (EG) improves implicit Q-learning (IQL) under cross-embodiment training. We compare across six datasets (Expert / Expert-Replay / 70% Suboptimal <math id="S6.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> Forward / Backward). Table <a href="#S6.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 6 Experimental Evaluation ‣ Cross-Embodiment Offline Reinforcement Learning for Heterogeneous Robot Datasets" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> reports the final returns, averaged over five random seeds with <math id="S6.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pm" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>±</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pm</annotation></semantics></math> indicating standard error. The variant that combines IQL with Embodiment Grouping achieves the best average performance. The gains are especially large when the dataset contains more suboptimal trajectories, as in the replay and 70% Suboptimal splits. Relative to methods that suppress gradient conflicts such as PCGrad and Selective Grouping (SEL), IQL+EG performs better. Compared to the IQL cross-embodiment baseline, the average improvement in the Suboptimal datasets 70% is 7.15% for PCGrad, 18.33% for SEL and 33.99% for EG.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">EG yields consistent benefits across a range of offline learning baselines. On the 70% Suboptimal datasets, applying EG to TD3+BC improves performance by +19.5% on average, raising the overall mean from 46.43 to 51.39. Similarly, BC+EG improves BC by +26.3% on the same suboptimal splits. These results indicate that embodiment-aware grouping remains broadly effective across different offline objectives. These improvements are most pronounced exactly in the regimes where Section <a href="#S5.SS1" title="5.1 Gradient Conflicts among Robots ‣ 5 Gradient Conflicts and Resolution via Embodiment-Based Grouping ‣ Cross-Embodiment Offline Reinforcement Learning for Heterogeneous Robot Datasets" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.1</span></a> revealed severe inter-robot gradient conflicts, supporting our hypothesis that embodiment-based grouping primarily helps by mitigating such conflicts across embodiments.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">6.2 </span>Ablations &amp; Compute-Normalized Analysis</h3>

<div id="S6.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This section disentangles design choices in Embodiment Grouping (EG) and the impact of compute. We examine: (i) grouping strategy, (ii) sensitivity to the number of groups <math id="S6.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math>, and (iii) comparisons where optimization steps and data usage are normalized.</p>
</div>
<section id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">(i) Grouping strategy</h5>

<figure id="S6.T4" class="ltx_table ltx_align_floatright" style="width:52%;">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 4: </span>Ablation on grouping strategy (70% Suboptimal Forward). <td id="S6.T4.2.5.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb"><span id="S6.T4.2.5.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">+38.34%</span></td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
</figure>
<div id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We compare clustering based on embodiment distance (FGW; Sec.<a href="#S5.SS2" title="5.2 Correlation between Embodiment Distance and the Gradient Conflicts ‣ 5 Gradient Conflicts and Resolution via Embodiment-Based Grouping ‣ Cross-Embodiment Offline Reinforcement Learning for Heterogeneous Robot Datasets" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.2</span></a>) (<span id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">EG</span>) against random partitioning (<span id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Random</span>) and an intuitive four-group split (<span id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Heuristic</span>: bipeds, quadrupeds, hexapods, and torso-less bipeds). Tab.<a href="#S6.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ (i) Grouping strategy ‣ 6.2 Ablations &amp; Compute-Normalized Analysis ‣ 6 Experimental Evaluation ‣ Cross-Embodiment Offline Reinforcement Learning for Heterogeneous Robot Datasets" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> reports the mean final return and variance on the 70% Suboptimal Forward dataset.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">From the table, <span id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">EG</span> achieves the most stable and substantial improvement on the 70% Suboptimal Forward dataset (+14.41, +38.34%). In contrast, <span id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Random</span> yields only a small gain (+1.16, +3.08%), and the intuitive four-way split <span id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Heuristic</span> actually degrades performance (-3.14, -8.31%). This trend is consistent with the correlation between reward gains and inter-robot gradient alignment shown in Sec. <a href="#S5.SS1" title="5.1 Gradient Conflicts among Robots ‣ 5 Gradient Conflicts and Resolution via Embodiment-Based Grouping ‣ Cross-Embodiment Offline Reinforcement Learning for Heterogeneous Robot Datasets" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.1</span></a>, indicating that EG, which groups by FGW-based distance, better aligns updates during training. It is somewhat surprising that the Heuristic split did not improve performance. A likely reason is that coarse categories such as leg count cannot capture gradient-relevant factors like actuator placement, link lengths, mass distribution, and joint couplings. By contrast, EG based on FGW distance forms groups that reflect structural and actuation similarity while maintaining sufficient data per group, thereby preserving within-group update consistency and suppressing gradient conflicts.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">(ii) Sensitivity to the group count <math id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math></h5>

<figure id="S6.F6" class="ltx_figure ltx_align_floatright" style="width:50%;"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18025v1/m_ablation_dual_axis_se.svg" id="S6.F6.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:274/146;" width="274" height="146"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 6: </span>Effect of the number of Embodiment Grouping clusters <math id="S6.F6.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> on final return and wall-clock training time (mean <math id="S6.F6.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pm" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>±</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pm</annotation></semantics></math> s.e.).</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate the effect of the number of Embodiment Grouping clusters <math id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> by sweeping <math id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> over <math id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{1,2,4,7,10,13\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>13</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{1,2,4,7,10,13\}</annotation></semantics></math>. The final performance as a function of <math id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> is plotted in Fig. <a href="#S6.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ (ii) Sensitivity to the group count 𝑀 ‣ 6.2 Ablations &amp; Compute-Normalized Analysis ‣ 6 Experimental Evaluation ‣ Cross-Embodiment Offline Reinforcement Learning for Heterogeneous Robot Datasets" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>; performance peaks at small to moderate <math id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math>, whereas excessive partitioning leads to a slight degradation (e.g., on the 70% Forward dataset the best score is attained at <math id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M{=}7" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>7</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M{=}7</annotation></semantics></math>). Because <math id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> also determines the number of policy updates per batch, smaller <math id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> reduces the number of updates and thus improves computational efficiency. As shown in
Fig. <a href="#S6.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ (ii) Sensitivity to the group count 𝑀 ‣ 6.2 Ablations &amp; Compute-Normalized Analysis ‣ 6 Experimental Evaluation ‣ Cross-Embodiment Offline Reinforcement Learning for Heterogeneous Robot Datasets" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>, the wall-clock training time grows substantially with <math id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math>. Taken together, these results suggest that relatively small values, <math id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M{=}2\!\sim\!4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo rspace="0.108em">=</mo><mphantom></mphantom><mo>∼</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M{=}2\!\sim\!4</annotation></semantics></math>, already yield strong gains; a practical strategy is to start with a small <math id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> and increase it gradually while balancing the trade-off between training time and performance.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">(iii) Compute- and data-normalized comparison</h5>

</table>
</figure>
<div id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">EG performs <math id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> policy updates per outer iteration, so a naive setup increases the number of updates by a factor of <math id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math>. The results above matched the total number of data steps but not the number of policy’s optimizer updates, which may be unfair. To remove this effect, we also run a compute-normalized comparison in which, for the IQL baseline, we multiply the total number of optimizer steps <math id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> by <math id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> to match EG, and reduce the batch size by <math id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1/M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1/M</annotation></semantics></math> so that the total number of processed samples remains constant. The results are summarized in Tab. <a href="#S6.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ (iii) Compute- and data-normalized comparison ‣ 6.2 Ablations &amp; Compute-Normalized Analysis ‣ 6 Experimental Evaluation ‣ Cross-Embodiment Offline Reinforcement Learning for Heterogeneous Robot Datasets" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>. We observe that with the 70% Suboptimal Forward dataset, the advantage of EG persists even after normalization. This indicates that the benefit of EG does not stem merely from increasing the number of policy updates, but rather from its grouping strategy that mitigates gradient interference.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S7" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">7 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S7.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We presented the systematic study of combining offline RL with cross-embodiment pre-training across 16 robot platforms. Our results show that this paradigm is particularly effective when datasets contain substantial suboptimal trajectories. On such datasets it achieves higher returns than BC, and for downstream adaptation it learns faster than training without cross-embodiment pre-training. We also identified a core failure mode, inter-robot gradient conflicts, whose incidence grows with both the proportion of suboptimal data and the number of embodiments. Quantifying gradient alignment showed a consistent association with transfer performance, and we found that this alignment is well captured by embodiment distance. This motivates our proposed Embodiment Grouping (EG), which clusters robots by morphology-aware distances and performs group-wise policy updates. EG consistently reduces interference and delivers the largest gains under high-suboptimal conditions.</p>
</div>
<div id="S7.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.p2.1" class="ltx_p">This study has limitations. Our evaluation is restricted to MuJoCo locomotion in simulation, which leaves sim-to-real transfer and broader domains such as manipulation and mobile manipulation untested. Our proposed Embodiment Grouping is static and derived from embodiment graphs using FGW distances. It works stably in offline RL, but it may not adapt when learning dynamics or data quality change, as in offline-to-online RL settings. Promising directions include validation on real robots and on manipulation tasks. Another direction is to improve Embodiment Grouping with dynamic grouping that uses embodiment information together with learning progress and data characteristics. In addition, once compatible groups are identified, learning group-specific embodiment or task representations within each group, for example using contrastive objectives <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yap and Koon Ng, 2024</a>)</cite>, could further strengthen within-group sharing. We leave this combined direction for future work.</p>
</div>
<section id="S7.SS0.SSSx1" class="ltx_subsubsection">

<section id="Sx1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section">Reproducibility Statement</h2>

<div id="Sx1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="Sx1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We ensure reproducibility via clear pointers. The grouped-update procedure appears in Algorithm <a href="#S5.SS3" title="5.3 Embodiment-Grouped Offline RL Update ‣ 5 Gradient Conflicts and Resolution via Embodiment-Based Grouping ‣ Cross-Embodiment Offline Reinforcement Learning for Heterogeneous Robot Datasets" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.3</span></a>. The architecture and training details are in Appendix <a href="#A4" title="Appendix D Architecture Details ‣ Cross-Embodiment Offline Reinforcement Learning for Heterogeneous Robot Datasets" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D</span></a>; Hyperparameters for BC, IQL, TD3+BC, and PPO are in Appendix <a href="#A9" title="Appendix I Hyperparameters and Training Details ‣ Cross-Embodiment Offline Reinforcement Learning for Heterogeneous Robot Datasets" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">I</span></a> and Tables <a href="#A9.T11" title="Table 11 ‣ I.1 IQL, BC, and TD3+BC Hyperparameters for Training ‣ Appendix I Hyperparameters and Training Details ‣ Cross-Embodiment Offline Reinforcement Learning for Heterogeneous Robot Datasets" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a> and <a href="#A9.T12" title="Table 12 ‣ I.2 PPO Hyperparameters for Dataset Generation ‣ Appendix I Hyperparameters and Training Details ‣ Cross-Embodiment Offline Reinforcement Learning for Heterogeneous Robot Datasets" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">12</span></a>. Dataset construction, including Expert, Expert Replay, and <math id="Sx1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X\%</annotation></semantics></math> Suboptimal, is in Appendix <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B Dataset Construction Details ‣ Cross-Embodiment Offline Reinforcement Learning for Heterogeneous Robot Datasets" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a>, with distributions of rewards in Appendix <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C Dataset Detail ‣ Cross-Embodiment Offline Reinforcement Learning for Heterogeneous Robot Datasets" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a>. Embodiment distance and clustering, including robot graphs and FGW settings, are in Appendix <a href="#A5" title="Appendix E Embodiment Grouping Details ‣ Cross-Embodiment Offline Reinforcement Learning for Heterogeneous Robot Datasets" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E</span></a> and Appendix <a href="#A5.SS2" title="E.2 Computing Fused Gromov–Wasserstein distance ‣ Appendix E Embodiment Grouping Details ‣ Cross-Embodiment Offline Reinforcement Learning for Heterogeneous Robot Datasets" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E.2</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>

<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>Use of Large Language Models (LLMs)</h2>

<p id="A1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We used LLMs to polish the writing of the paper and perform grammar checks.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix B </span>Dataset Construction Details</h2>

<div id="A2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This appendix describes how each dataset used in our experiments was constructed.</p>
</div>
<section id="A2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.1 </span>Expert Dataset</h3>

<figure id="A2.F7" class="ltx_figure ltx_align_floatright" style="width:36%;"><img src="2602.18025v1/Go2ForwardBackward.png" id="A2.F7.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:198/97;" width="198" height="97" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 7: </span>Illustration of the Forward and Backward locomotion commands used in our datasets.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The <span id="A2.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Expert</span> dataset was collected using an expert model that can walk almost perfectly according to a given command. For each robot, we independently trained a PPO policy to convergence and used it to generate data. Starting from the environment’s default initial state, we sampled actions from the Gaussian distribution predicted by the trained policy to log trajectories. We illustrate the
<span id="A2.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Forward</span> and <span id="A2.SS1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Backward</span> locomotion commands in Figure <a href="#A2.F7" title="Figure 7 ‣ B.1 Expert Dataset ‣ Appendix B Dataset Construction Details ‣ Cross-Embodiment Offline Reinforcement Learning for Heterogeneous Robot Datasets" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>. For the Forward dataset, we issued a command to walk forward at <math id="A2.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1\,\mathrm{m/s}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow><mo>/</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1\,\mathrm{m/s}</annotation></semantics></math>; for the Backward dataset, we issued a command to walk backward at <math id="A2.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1\,\mathrm{m/s}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow><mo>/</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1\,\mathrm{m/s}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.2 </span>Expert Replay Dataset</h3>

<div id="A2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The <span id="A2.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Expert Replay</span> dataset contains interaction data collected from the beginning of training up to the point at which the model can walk according to the given command (e.g., move forward at <math id="A2.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1\,\mathrm{m/s}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow><mo>/</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1\,\mathrm{m/s}</annotation></semantics></math> for the <span id="A2.SS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Forward</span> condition). Storing all PPO interaction data is impractical due to PPO’s low sample efficiency, which would result in extremely large data volume and step counts. We therefore constructed a uniformly thinned <math id="A2.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1\,\mathrm{M}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1\,\mathrm{M}</annotation></semantics></math>-step dataset via the following procedure:</p>
</div>
<section id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">(1) Environment selection and full logging.</h5>

<div id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Among the 48 parallel environments used for training, we selected one and fully recorded all rollouts (approximately <math id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10\,\mathrm{M}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>10</mn><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10\,\mathrm{M}</annotation></semantics></math> steps) in that environment, thereby capturing trajectories from the initial exploration phase through to near convergence.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">(2) Extract data up to just before convergence.</h5>

<div id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">From the saved logs, we reconstructed episode boundaries and computed each episode’s return and length. We then applied a moving average to episode returns and identified the first point at which performance reached <math id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="90\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>90</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">90\%</annotation></semantics></math> of the final performance. Data up to just before this point were retained as the candidate set, while the subsequent steps, during which performance increases only slowly toward full convergence, were omitted.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">(3) Uniform thinning to <math id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1\,\mathrm{M}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1\,\mathrm{M}</annotation></semantics></math> steps.</h5>

<div id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">If the total number of steps in the candidate set exceeded <math id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1\,\mathrm{M}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1\,\mathrm{M}</annotation></semantics></math>, we down-sampled by discarding episodes at equal intervals with respect to cumulative steps. This preserved the overall distribution while reducing the dataset to approximately <math id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1\,\mathrm{M}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1\,\mathrm{M}</annotation></semantics></math> steps.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Using this shared procedure, we created the replay datasets for all robots. For the <span id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Forward</span> datasets of Unitree A1, Go1, and Go2, the default PPO hyperparameters led to local optima. To encourage exploration and avoid such local optima, we trained these policies with an increased policy entropy coefficient, <math id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\texttt{entropy\_coef}=0.1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">entropy_coef</mtext><mo>=</mo><mn>0.1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\texttt{entropy\_coef}=0.1</annotation></semantics></math>, and used the resulting data.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.3 </span><math id="A2.SS3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X\%</annotation></semantics></math> Suboptimal Dataset</h3>

<div id="A2.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The <math id="A2.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X\%</annotation></semantics></math> Suboptimal dataset is constructed so that <math id="A2.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X\%</annotation></semantics></math> of the data are suboptimal. In particular, the <math id="A2.SS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="70\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>70</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">70\%</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A2.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic"> Suboptimal</span> dataset used in our experiments contains a relatively large proportion of suboptimal trajectories. Whereas the Replay dataset samples evenly from early to late training phases, the <math id="A2.SS3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X\%</annotation></semantics></math> Suboptimal dataset is formed by sampling <math id="A2.SS3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X\%</annotation></semantics></math> from the early training phase and <math id="A2.SS3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="100\!-\!X\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">100\!-\!X\%</annotation></semantics></math> from the late training phase.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.4 </span>Reward Function</h3>

<div id="A2.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We construct our datasets by following the walking-task setup of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bohlinger et al. (2024)</a></cite> and adopt a dense locomotion reward that encourages accurate tracking of commanded base velocities while penalizing undesirable gait patterns. The reward is composed of two command-tracking terms defined with respect to the target velocities <math id="A2.SS4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>c</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c</annotation></semantics></math>, together with several penalty terms that shape the gait. Each term is weighted by its own coefficient, and the total reward is obtained by summing all weighted terms and clipping the result from below at zero. Tables <a href="#A2.T6" title="Table 6 ‣ B.4 Reward Function ‣ Appendix B Dataset Construction Details ‣ Cross-Embodiment Offline Reinforcement Learning for Heterogeneous Robot Datasets" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> and <a href="#A2.T7" title="Table 7 ‣ B.4 Reward Function ‣ Appendix B Dataset Construction Details ‣ Cross-Embodiment Offline Reinforcement Learning for Heterogeneous Robot Datasets" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> list the equations for each component of the reward function and the corresponding coefficients.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A2.T6" class="ltx_table">
<table id="A2.T6.2" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_guessed_headers ltx_align_middle">
<thead class="ltx_thead">
<tr id="A2.T6.2.1" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="A2.T6.2.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_t">Term</th>

<td id="A2.T7.2.1.17.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_b">2.0</td>
<td id="A2.T7.2.1.17.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_b">0.05</td>
<td id="A2.T7.2.1.17.6" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_b">0.2</td>
<td id="A2.T7.2.1.17.7" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_b">0.0</td>

</tbody>
</table>
</span></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 7: </span>Reward coefficients <math id="A2.T7.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r_{c}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r_{c}</annotation></semantics></math> and curriculum length <math id="A2.T7.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math> for each robot.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A3" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix C </span>Dataset Detail</h2>

<div id="A3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#A3.F8" title="Figure 8 ‣ Appendix C Dataset Detail ‣ Cross-Embodiment Offline Reinforcement Learning for Heterogeneous Robot Datasets" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a> overlays histograms of the total reward per episode for the Forward datasets, comparing the three data quality levels used throughout the paper: Expert Forward, Expert Replay Forward, and 70% Suboptimal Forward.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Overall, three consistent patterns emerge:
(i) <span id="A3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Expert</span> datasets are sharply concentrated at higher returns, indicating that most episodes achieve near-target performance;
(ii) <span id="A3.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Expert Replay</span> exhibits a broad spread that reflects a mixture of early failures and late competent behavior accumulated during training;
(iii) <span id="A3.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">70% Suboptimal</span> shifts mass toward lower returns, with many episodes clustered near the low-reward region. Notably, while the 70% Suboptimal dataset contains only a small fraction of high-return episodes, those episodes tend to be considerably longer; when weighting by time steps, they account for approximately 30% of all steps.
We observe qualitatively similar distributions for the Backward datasets.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">These distributional differences clarify why offline RL tends to outperform pure imitation when suboptimal data are abundant: objectives that reweight actions by estimated advantages can discount low-quality behaviors while still leveraging recoverable structure present in Replay and Suboptimal corpora.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A3.F8" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18025v1/episode_hist_grid_4x4.svg" id="A3.F8.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:548/352;" width="548" height="352"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 8: </span>Overlaid histograms of per-episode total reward (x-axis) vs. episode proportion (y-axis) for Forward datasets across all robots. Each panel corresponds to a robot; colors denote Expert, Expert replay, and 70% Suboptimal. Expert concentrates at high returns, Replay spans a wide range, and 70% Suboptimal places substantial mass on low returns. Vertical solid line: median; vertical dashed lines: 25th and 75th percentiles.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="A4" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix D </span>Architecture Details</h2>

<section id="A4.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Encoder (URMA).</h5>

<div id="A4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We split each observation into general <math id="A4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="o_{g}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>g</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">o_{g}</annotation></semantics></math> and robot-specific streams. For locomotion, the observation vector is subdivided into joint- and foot-level sets
<math id="A4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{o_{j}\}_{j\in J(\tau)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mi>J</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{o_{j}\}_{j\in J(\tau)}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{o_{f}\}_{f\in F(\tau)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>f</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{o_{f}\}_{f\in F(\tau)}</annotation></semantics></math> with per-item descriptors <math id="A4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{j},d_{f}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>f</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{j},d_{f}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Descriptors and observations are encoded by MLPs <math id="A4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{\phi}:\mathbb{R}^{\cdot}\!\to\!\mathbb{R}^{L_{d}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mo>⋅</mo></msup><mo rspace="0.108em" stretchy="false">→</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>d</mi></msub></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{\phi}:\mathbb{R}^{\cdot}\!\to\!\mathbb{R}^{L_{d}}</annotation></semantics></math> and
<math id="A4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{\psi}:\mathbb{R}^{\cdot}\!\to\!\mathbb{R}^{L_{d}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>ψ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mo>⋅</mo></msup><mo rspace="0.108em" stretchy="false">→</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>d</mi></msub></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{\psi}:\mathbb{R}^{\cdot}\!\to\!\mathbb{R}^{L_{d}}</annotation></semantics></math>.
URMA uses descriptor-conditioned attention that gates each latent dimension:</p>
<table id="A4.EGx1" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="A4.E3"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A4.E3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\bar{z}_{\mathrm{joints}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>z</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mi>joints</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\bar{z}_{\mathrm{joints}}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A4.E3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=\sum_{j\in J}z_{j}," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><munder><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>J</mi></mrow></munder></mstyle><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\sum_{j\in J}z_{j},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A4.E3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\qquad z_{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\qquad z_{j}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A4.E3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=\frac{\exp\!\left(\dfrac{f_{\phi}(d_{j})}{\tau+\epsilon}\right)}{\displaystyle\sum_{L_{d}}\exp\!\left(\dfrac{f_{\phi}(d_{j})}{\tau+\epsilon}\right)}\;f_{\psi}(o_{j})." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mpadded style="width:1.370em;" width="1.370em"><mi>exp</mi></mpadded><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>ϵ</mi></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><munder><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>d</mi></msub></munder></mstyle><mrow><mpadded style="width:1.370em;" width="1.370em"><mi>exp</mi></mpadded><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>ϵ</mi></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo lspace="0.280em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>ψ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\frac{\exp\!\left(\dfrac{f_{\phi}(d_{j})}{\tau+\epsilon}\right)}{\displaystyle\sum_{L_{d}}\exp\!\left(\dfrac{f_{\phi}(d_{j})}{\tau+\epsilon}\right)}\;f_{\psi}(o_{j}).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">In the same way, we obtain <math id="A4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bar{z}_{\mathrm{feet}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>z</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mi>feet</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{z}_{\mathrm{feet}}</annotation></semantics></math> from <math id="A4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{o_{f},d_{f}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>f</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>f</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{o_{f},d_{f}\}</annotation></semantics></math>, and finally form a single latent vector by concatenation
<math id="A4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bar{z}=\mathrm{concat}\big[o_{g},\bar{z}_{\mathrm{joints}},\bar{z}_{\mathrm{feet}}\big]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>z</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>concat</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">[</mo><mrow><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>g</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>z</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mi>joints</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>z</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mi>feet</mi></msub></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{z}=\mathrm{concat}\big[o_{g},\bar{z}_{\mathrm{joints}},\bar{z}_{\mathrm{feet}}\big]</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A4.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Actor network.</h5>

<div id="A4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A core MLP <math id="A4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> maps the encoder output to an action latent:</p>
<table id="A4.E4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A4.E4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bar{z}_{\text{action}}=h_{\theta}(\bar{z})." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>z</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mtext>action</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>z</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{z}_{\text{action}}=h_{\theta}(\bar{z}).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">Per joint, the action head decodes Gaussian parameters from the tuple (encoded descriptor, joint latent, action latent) and samples an action:</p>
<table id="A4.Ex1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A4.Ex1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a^{j}\sim\mathcal{N}\!\big(\mu_{\nu}(d_{j}^{a},\ \bar{z}_{\mathrm{action}},\ z_{j}),\ \sigma_{\nu}(d_{j}^{a})\big),\qquad d_{j}^{a}=g_{\omega}(d_{j})." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>a</mi><mi>j</mi></msup><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mpadded style="width:0.798em;" width="0.798em"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi></mpadded><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>μ</mi><mi>ν</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>d</mi><mi>j</mi><mi>a</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>z</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mi>action</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>ν</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>d</mi><mi>j</mi><mi>a</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="2.167em">,</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>d</mi><mi>j</mi><mi>a</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>g</mi><mi>ω</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a^{j}\sim\mathcal{N}\!\big(\mu_{\nu}(d_{j}^{a},\ \bar{z}_{\mathrm{action}},\ z_{j}),\ \sigma_{\nu}(d_{j}^{a})\big),\qquad d_{j}^{a}=g_{\omega}(d_{j}).</annotation></semantics></math></td>

</table>
<p id="A4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.3" class="ltx_p">Here <math id="A4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu_{\nu}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>μ</mi><mi>ν</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu_{\nu}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma_{\nu}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>ν</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_{\nu}</annotation></semantics></math> are MLPs.</p>

</section>
<section id="A4.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">State value network.</h5>

<div id="A4.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The state value network uses the encoder and predicts a state value from the latent:</p>
<table id="A4.E5" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>

</table>
<p id="A4.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.2" class="ltx_p">implemented as an MLP (e.g., <math id="A4.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[512,256,128]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>512,256,128</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[512,256,128]</annotation></semantics></math>).</p>
</div>

<section id="A4.SS0.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">State–action value Network</h5>

<div id="A4.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For offline RL, we add an action encoder <math id="A4.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{a}:\mathbb{R}^{d_{a}}\!\to\!\mathbb{R}^{L_{a}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>a</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>a</mi></msub></msup><mo rspace="0.108em" stretchy="false">→</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>a</mi></msub></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{a}:\mathbb{R}^{d_{a}}\!\to\!\mathbb{R}^{L_{a}}</annotation></semantics></math> and form a joint latent for <math id="A4.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Q" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>Q</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
<table id="A4.EGx2" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="A4.E6"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A4.E6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle z_{a}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>a</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle z_{a}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A4.E6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=f_{a}(a),\qquad Q_{\eta}^{(k)}(\bar{z},a)\;=\;q_{\eta}^{(k)}\!\big(\mathrm{concat}[\bar{z},\ z_{a}]\big),\quad k\in\{1,2\}." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>a</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="2.167em">,</mo><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>Q</mi><mi>η</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>z</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo rspace="0.280em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.558em">=</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>q</mi><mi>η</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><mrow><mi>concat</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>z</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mo rspace="0.667em">,</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>a</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=f_{a}(a),\qquad Q_{\eta}^{(k)}(\bar{z},a)\;=\;q_{\eta}^{(k)}\!\big(\mathrm{concat}[\bar{z},\ z_{a}]\big),\quad k\in\{1,2\}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(6)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A4.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.2" class="ltx_p">To accommodate heterogeneous action sizes, we feed <math id="A4.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{a}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>a</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{a}</annotation></semantics></math> a zero-padded action vector <math id="A4.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{a}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\max}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>a</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>max</mi></msub></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{a}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\max}}</annotation></semantics></math> (padded to the maximum action length across robots).</p>
</div>

</section>
</section>
<section id="A5" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix E </span>Embodiment Grouping Details</h2>

<div id="A5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This appendix gives a detailed recipe for grouping robots when building the embodiment distance used by our method. We first define the robot graph representation. We then list the node features and hyperparameters used to compute the Fused Gromov-Wasserstein distance.</p>
</div>
<section id="A5.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">E.1 </span>Robot graph representation</h3>

<div id="A5.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A5.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We represent each robot as a graph. The nodes correspond to the torso the joints and the feet. The edges connect the torso to adjacent joints adjacent joints to each other and the terminal joint to its foot. Figure <a href="#A5.F10" title="Figure 10 ‣ E.1 Robot graph representation ‣ Appendix E Embodiment Grouping Details ‣ Cross-Embodiment Offline Reinforcement Learning for Heterogeneous Robot Datasets" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a> shows images of all robots and the corresponding graph representation. Each node carries a feature vector constructed from the local descriptors that URMA uses as encoder inputs.
The graph features are derived from the same observation factorization that URMA assumes: the joint-level and foot-level sets <math id="A5.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{o_{j}\}_{j\in J(\tau)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mi>J</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{o_{j}\}_{j\in J(\tau)}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A5.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{o_{f}\}_{f\in F(\tau)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>f</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{o_{f}\}_{f\in F(\tau)}</annotation></semantics></math> with their corresponding local descriptors
<math id="A5.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{d_{j}\}_{j\in J(\tau)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mi>J</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{d_{j}\}_{j\in J(\tau)}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A5.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{d_{f}\}_{f\in F(\tau)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>f</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{d_{f}\}_{f\in F(\tau)}</annotation></semantics></math>, together with a general observation stream. In our embodiment graphs, only the local descriptors <math id="A5.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{d_{j}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{d_{j}\}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A5.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{d_{f}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>f</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{d_{f}\}</annotation></semantics></math> are used as node attributes;
importantly, we do not use URMA’s learned latent embeddings directly as graph node features. In particular, joint nodes use the joint descriptor <math id="A5.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{j}</annotation></semantics></math>, foot nodes use the foot descriptor <math id="A5.SS1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{f}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>f</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{f}</annotation></semantics></math>, and the torso node receives a zero vector of the same dimension. The shared observation decomposition between URMA and the embodiment graphs can be viewed as an inductive bias that helps Embodiment Grouping mitigate gradient conflicts. When applying embodiment grouping with policy architectures other than URMA, it may therefore be beneficial to design graph node features so that they respect the observation factorization implied by the chosen policy architecture.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A5.F10" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18025v1/all_robots_grid.png" id="A5.F10.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:548/370;" width="548" height="370" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 10: </span>All robots with their images and the corresponding graph representation. Nodes are torso joints and feet. Edges follow kinematic adjacency and the connection from each terminal joint to its foot.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="A5.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">E.2 </span>Computing Fused Gromov–Wasserstein distance</h3>

<div id="A5.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A5.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We compute pairwise distances between robot graphs using the Fused Gromov–Wasserstein distance with the POT library <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Flamary et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. Feature costs use the Euclidean norm on standardized descriptors. Structural costs use shortest path distances on each graph. Node weights are uniform over nodes in each graph. Table <a href="#A5.T8" title="Table 8 ‣ E.2 Computing Fused Gromov–Wasserstein distance ‣ Appendix E Embodiment Grouping Details ‣ Cross-Embodiment Offline Reinforcement Learning for Heterogeneous Robot Datasets" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a> lists the hyperparameters that were fixed for all pairs.</p>
</div>
<div id="A5.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A5.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We next discuss how this computation scales with the number of embodiments.
In our method, FGW is used only to compute pairwise distances between embodiments before training, in order to build the embodiment distance matrix.
As the number of robots <math id="A5.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math> increases, the number of FGW computations grows with the number of pairs, which is <math id="A5.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\binom{N}{2}=N(N-1)/2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo>(</mo><mfrac linethickness="0pt"><mi>N</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\binom{N}{2}=N(N-1)/2</annotation></semantics></math>. Thus, the overall complexity for building the distance matrix is <math id="A5.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(N^{2})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>N</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(N^{2})</annotation></semantics></math>. In practice, this cost is small compared to policy training. For our 16-robot setup, computing the full <math id="A5.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="16\times 16" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>16</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>16</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">16\times 16</annotation></semantics></math> distance matrix with our POT-based implementation takes about 0.8 seconds on a standard machine.
Even for substantially larger <math id="A5.SS2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math>, this one-time cost remains negligible relative to the offline RL training time.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A5.T8" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 8: </span>Essential hyperparameters for Fused Gromov–Wasserstein distance with POT</figcaption>
<table id="A5.T8.2" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_guessed_headers ltx_align_middle">
<tbody class="ltx_tbody">
<tr id="A5.T8.2.1" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="A5.T8.2.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row ltx_border_tt">Parameter</th>
<td id="A5.T8.2.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_tt">Setting</td></tr>
<tr id="A5.T8.2.2" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="A5.T8.2.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row ltx_border_t">Feature ground metric</th>
<td id="A5.T8.2.2.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_t">Euclidean distance</td></tr>

<td id="A5.T8.2.4.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left"><math id="A5.T8.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.5</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.5</annotation></semantics></math></td></tr>

<td id="A5.T8.2.5.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_bb"><math id="A5.T8.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1\mathrm{e}{-3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1\mathrm{e}{-3}</annotation></semantics></math></td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="A5.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">E.3 </span>Resulting Group Assignments</h3>

<div id="A5.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A5.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Using the FGW distance matrix described above, we perform hierarchical agglomerative clustering and cut the dendrogram to obtain <math id="A5.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> groups.
Figure <a href="#A5.F11" title="Figure 11 ‣ E.3 Resulting Group Assignments ‣ Appendix E Embodiment Grouping Details ‣ Cross-Embodiment Offline Reinforcement Learning for Heterogeneous Robot Datasets" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a> visualizes the resulting robot partitions for <math id="A5.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M=2,4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M=2,4</annotation></semantics></math>. These assignments are computed once from the FGW distance matrix and kept fixed across all experiments.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A5.F11" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="A5.F11.sf1" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><img src="2602.18025v1/eg_m2.png" id="A5.F11.sf1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:548/260;" width="548" height="260" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">(a) </span><math id="A5.F11.sf1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M=2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M=2</annotation></semantics></math></figcaption>
</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">

</section>

<section id="A6" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix F </span>Detailed analysis of gradient conflicts</h2>

<div id="A6.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We further analyze gradient conflicts by collecting the pairwise cosine similarities <math id="A6.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C[\tau_{i},\tau_{j}]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msub><mi>τ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>τ</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C[\tau_{i},\tau_{j}]</annotation></semantics></math> for all robot pairs and training steps, and aggregating them into histograms (see Figure <a href="#A6.F12" title="Figure 12 ‣ Appendix F Detailed analysis of gradient conflicts ‣ Cross-Embodiment Offline Reinforcement Learning for Heterogeneous Robot Datasets" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">12</span></a>). Two consistent trends emerge:</p>
</div>
<div id="A6.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A6.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A6.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(i) Effect of suboptimal data.</span> As the proportion of suboptimal trajectories increases, the fraction of pairs with <math id="A6.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C&lt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C&lt;0</annotation></semantics></math> grows. Moreover, within the negative region (<math id="A6.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C&lt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C&lt;0</annotation></semantics></math>), the share of values close to <math id="A6.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-1</annotation></semantics></math> increases with the proportion of suboptimal data, indicating a stronger misalignment per update and a higher probability of negative transfer. Consistently, the mean cosine <math id="A6.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bar{C}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>C</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{C}</annotation></semantics></math> decreases as the suboptimal fraction increases. Overall, these results show that increasing suboptimal data makes gradient conflicts both more frequent and more severe.</p>
</div>
<div id="A6.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A6.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A6.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(ii) Effect of embodiment diversity.</span> As we include more and more diverse embodiments, the fraction of pairs with <math id="A6.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C&lt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C&lt;0</annotation></semantics></math> increases, while the share of strongly aligned pairs (large positive <math id="A6.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>C</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C</annotation></semantics></math>) diminishes. The mean cosine <math id="A6.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bar{C}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>C</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{C}</annotation></semantics></math> also gradually declines as the embodiment diversity increases. Together, these effects indicate that greater embodiment diversity amplifies gradient conflicts, thereby increasing negative transfer and making positive transfer less likely.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A6.F12" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="A6.F12.sf1" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><img src="2602.18025v1/images/grad_inner_histogram_overlay_70_30_expert.png" id="A6.F12.sf1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:548/411;" width="548" height="411" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">(a) </span>Varying suboptimal-data proportion.</figcaption>
</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="A6.F12.sf2" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><img src="2602.18025v1/images/grad_inner_histogram_overlay_70_variants.png" id="A6.F12.sf2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:548/411;" width="548" height="411" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">(b) </span>Varying embodiment diversity.</figcaption>
</figure></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 12: </span><span id="A6.F12.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Histograms of pairwise cosine similarities</span> <math id="A6.F12.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C[\tau_{i},\tau_{j}]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msub><mi>τ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>τ</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C[\tau_{i},\tau_{j}]</annotation></semantics></math> aggregated over training.
In both settings—(a) higher suboptimal-data ratios and (b) greater embodiment diversity—the fraction with <math id="A6.F12.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C&lt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C&lt;0</annotation></semantics></math> increases; within <math id="A6.F12.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C&lt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C&lt;0</annotation></semantics></math>, mass concentrates at more negative values. Solid lines indicate the mean <math id="A6.F12.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bar{C}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>C</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{C}</annotation></semantics></math>.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
